opus-5.5.text:
I think user interface design is one of the most underappreciated parts of responsible AI. We spend a lot of time talking about the model, the training data, and the safety systems around it, but ultimately people experience these systems through the interface. That's where expectations get set, and that's where a lot of the real-world risk either gets mitigated or amplified.

One of the biggest challenges with generative AI is that it's very fluent. It sounds confident even when it's wrong, and people naturally tend to over-rely on something that communicates so well. So a key job of the UX is to help people calibrate their trust appropriately. That can mean being transparent that they're interacting with AI, setting expectations up front about what the system is good at and where it might make mistakes, and making it easy to verify what it says. For example, when a system grounds its answers in sources, showing citations right there in the response lets people click through and check. That changes the experience from "trust me" to "here's where this came from."

Another important pattern is keeping the human in the loop and in control. In a lot of scenarios, we design the experience so the AI produces a draft, and the person reviews, edits, and decides what to do with it. The framing matters. When we call something a "copilot," we're signaling that you're still the pilot. You're accountable for the final output, and the system is there to help you go faster, not replace your judgment.

We also think about friction in a really intentional way. Usually product design is about removing friction, but sometimes a little friction is exactly what you want. That might be a prompt to review content before it's sent, or limits on how long a conversation can run, because we've seen that very long sessions can push models into unexpected territory. It might be a clear way to give feedback or report a problem, so people can flag issues and we can keep improving.

Finally, a lot of this is about helping people learn how to use a new kind of tool. Generative AI is very open-ended, and many people don't know what to ask or how to get good results. Suggested prompts, examples, and gentle guidance in the interface help people discover useful capabilities and steer them away from uses the system isn't designed for. Good UX is really one layer in a defense-in-depth approach. Alongside the model and the safety systems, it makes the whole system more useful and more responsible at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI fluency, mistakes, and risk, but does not mention beneficial surprises or interface messaging about them.

r002.rationale: It describes drafts, review, and user control, but does not explain selectable response modes that adapt behavior to the intended task.

r003.rationale: It says citations let users click through and check sources, but does not connect confidence in an answer to the user's judgment of the sources' authority.

r004.rationale: It calls interface design “one of the most underappreciated parts” and contrasts it with the time spent discussing the model, clearly conveying that UI receives less attention than model-focused work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think UI is honestly one of the most underrated levers we have in responsible AI right now. We spend a lot of time talking about the model, and the model matters, but the interface is where a person actually forms their mental model of what this thing is and what it can do. And with generative AI, that mental model is often wrong by default.

The core challenge is that these systems are incredibly fluent. They sound confident, they sound authoritative, and people naturally calibrate to that tone. So if you just drop a chat box in front of someone, they'll tend to over-trust it. A lot of what good interface design does here is counteract that. It's about helping people understand that this is a tool that produces plausible output, not a source of truth, and giving them the affordances to verify, to steer, and to recover when it gets something wrong.

Concretely, a few things we've learned matter a lot. First, grounding and citations. When the system shows where an answer came from, people can check it, and it changes the interaction from "believe me" to "here's what I found, go look." Second, making the boundaries visible. Explaining up front what the system is designed for and what it's not, and being honest in the moment when it's uncertain or can't do something, rather than confabulating. Third, keeping the human in a position of agency. Features like suggested follow-ups, the ability to edit and regenerate, showing drafts rather than final answers. All of that frames the AI as a collaborator you're directing, not an oracle you're consulting.

And then there's the feedback loop. The interface is also how we learn. Thumbs up, thumbs down, "this was wrong," those signals are how the system gets better, and they're also how users feel like they have some control over the experience.

What I'd really emphasize, though, is that you can't bolt this on at the end. The responsible AI work and the design work have to happen together. A lot of the harms we worry about, over-reliance, misinformation, people being misled about what they're interacting with, those aren't purely model problems. They're product problems, and the interface is where you solve them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and plausible output but does not identify beneficial surprises as part of AI unpredictability or say that interface messaging should communicate them.

r002.rationale: It mentions suggested follow-ups and editing or regenerating, but does not explain how user-selectable response modes align system behavior with the intended task.

r003.rationale: It says citations let users check where an answer came from, but does not explain that users assess confidence by judging the sources’ authority.

r004.rationale: Calling UI an underrated lever and contrasting it with how much attention goes to the model communicates that interface design receives less attention than model-focused work.

astra-6.text:
I think interface design is a really important part of helping people build the right mental model of these systems. When you see a beautifully written answer, it’s easy to assume that the system knows what it’s talking about. But fluency and correctness are different things, and the interface needs to help you understand that without making the product difficult to use.

One way to do that is to make verification part of the workflow. If the system is answering a question based on documents, can you easily see the relevant source and check whether it supports the answer? If it’s taking an action, can you preview what it’s going to do and correct it before it proceeds? Those design choices give people practical control.

There’s also an opportunity to help people discover what’s possible. A blank text box is incredibly flexible, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you where to start. Examples, suggested next steps, and ways to refine an answer can help people get value without having to become experts in prompting.

The goal is to help people develop appropriate trust: understand where the system is useful, where they need to check its work, and how to steer it when it hasn’t understood what they want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verification and appropriate trust, but does not identify beneficial surprises as an aspect of AI unpredictability or say interface messaging can communicate them.

r002.rationale: It mentions examples and ways to refine an answer, but does not explain that users can select response modes to match the system’s behavior to their task.

r003.rationale: It says users can check whether a cited source supports an answer, but does not connect confidence to the user’s judgment of the source’s authority.

r004.rationale: The response does not compare attention to interface design with attention to model alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the user interface is a huge part of helping people build the right mental model of these systems. A blank text box is incredibly flexible, but it doesn’t tell you much about what you can do, what context you should provide, or how to judge the response. So even something as simple as showing examples or helping someone refine their request can make a big difference.

And then, on the output side, how do we make it easy to check the answer? If the system is using source material, can you see those sources and understand whether they actually support what it said? Can you edit the result, ask a follow-up, or correct an assumption without starting over?

We want people to benefit from the capabilities without assuming that a fluent answer is necessarily a correct answer. You can put a warning somewhere, but I think the more useful approach is to build that understanding into the interaction itself—to make verification and human judgment a natural part of using the product.
